subtitle: Abraham, Jacob, Joseph, and the Promise That Holds
description: Genesis 12–50 traces a single thread: God's covenant promise moving through broken, ordinary people. Watch the Bible Project's animated overview, then spend four days sitting with what it means to be chosen, to wrestle, to suffer, and to forgive.

aboutSource.name: The Bible Project
aboutSource.description: The Bible Project creates free animated videos, podcasts, and educational resources that explore the Bible as a unified story leading to Jesus. Their goal is to help people read the Bible with depth and clarity.

days.title: Go
days.center: As you enter this reflection, ask yourself: is there anything God has been prompting you toward that you've been reluctant to step into? Hold that lightly as you begin.
days.watchPrompt: Think back to how the video framed Abraham's call — God's promise starts with one man but is aimed at every family on earth. What does the video reveal about what it actually means to be chosen by God?
days.reflectionQuestion: God chose Abraham not just to bless him but to make him a blessing to all people — how does that shape your understanding of what God's call on your own life is actually for?

scripture.text: The Lord said to Abram, 'Leave your land, your people, and your father's household, and go to the land I will show you. I will make you into a great nation. I will bless you and make your name great, so that you will be a blessing. I will bless those who bless you and oppose those who oppose you. Through you, all the families of the earth will be blessed.'

crossReferences.reason: Paul reveals that the gospel itself was announced in advance through this promise — blessing through faith was always God's plan from the beginning.
Abraham obeyed without knowing where he was going — his faith was in the person making the promise, not the clarity of the plan.
Peter quotes this promise directly after the resurrection — showing that the Abrahamic blessing finds its fulfillment in Christ Jesus.

days.abideInsight: Abraham didn't know where he was going. He left behind everything familiar and set out on the word of a God he was only beginning to know. What's striking is that God's promise wasn't primarily about Abraham's comfort or achievement — it was about the world being restored through him. Being chosen by God has never been about personal privilege. It has always been about becoming a channel for something larger than yourself. The call to go is still the call.
days.actionStep: Identify one person, community, or context beyond your immediate circle — a neighbor, a coworker, a place you pass daily — and take one concrete step this week to bring blessing into their life. It doesn't have to be large. It has to be intentional.
days.prayer: God, you called Abraham to leave what was comfortable and go toward what was unknown. I want to hold my plans loosely the same way. Show me who I'm supposed to be a blessing to — and give me the courage to actually go.

days.title: The Wrestler
days.center: Come honest today. You don't have to perform spiritual readiness. Just show up with whatever is actually true about where you are right now.
days.watchPrompt: Think back to how the video portrayed Jacob — a man who tried to grab through cunning what only God could give. Notice that God doesn't wait for people to be clean before he works through them. What did the wrestling scene reveal about what transformation costs?
days.reflectionQuestion: What is the place in your life where you are most resistant to yielding to God — and what do you think you're protecting by holding on?

scripture.text: The man said, 'Let me go — the dawn is breaking.' But Jacob said, 'I will not let you go unless you bless me.' The man asked him, 'What is your name?' He replied, 'Jacob.' Then the man said, 'Your name will no longer be Jacob, but Israel — for you have striven with God and with people, and you have prevailed.'

crossReferences.reason: Hosea looks back at this very moment — Jacob wrestling, weeping, seeking God's favor — as a model of what real repentance and longing for God look like.
Paul uses Jacob's story to show that God's choosing isn't based on human merit — grace runs deeper than behavior or achievement.
Paul's image of pressing on to take hold of what Christ has taken hold of carries the same spirit as Jacob refusing to let go without the blessing.

days.abideInsight: Jacob spent his whole life trying to seize through his own strength what only God could give. His wrestling match wasn't a victory of force — it was the moment he finally broke. His limp wasn't something to be ashamed of; it was evidence that he had been close enough to God to be changed. Transformation in Scripture almost always comes through struggle, not comfort. God doesn't prize the person who never wrestles — he gives new names to people who refuse to walk away without a blessing.
days.actionStep: Spend ten minutes in honest, unfiltered prayer about the specific thing you most resist surrendering to God. Don't dress it up. Don't try to resolve it. Just bring it and stay there.
days.prayer: God, there are things I'm gripping that I don't want to let go of. I don't fully trust you with them yet. Like Jacob, I need you to meet me in the struggle. I'm not walking away without a blessing.

days.title: In the Pit
days.center: If you're carrying something painful right now, you don't have to set it aside to be here. Bring it. This story was written for people in exactly your situation.
days.watchPrompt: Recall how the video handled Joseph's story — God's name is absent in the darkest chapters, yet the narrator keeps telling us he was there. How does the Bible Project frame the difference between God causing suffering and God being present inside it?
days.reflectionQuestion: Looking back on a chapter of your life that felt like God was absent — what do you now see, or what are you learning to trust, about where God actually was?

scripture.text: Joseph's master had him thrown into prison — the place where the king's prisoners were kept. But while Joseph was there in prison, the Lord was with him. He extended kindness to him and gave him favor in the eyes of the prison warden.

crossReferences.reason: The psalmist retells Joseph's story and highlights that God's word was testing him in the suffering — the pain had purpose even when Joseph couldn't see it.
Paul's confidence that God works all things together for good finds its deepest Old Testament illustration in the story of Joseph.
God's promise to be present through fire and deep water echoes what is woven through Joseph's story — suffering did not mean abandonment.

days.abideInsight: What makes the Joseph story so honest is that it doesn't sanitize the suffering. The pit was real. The betrayal was real. The years of wrongful imprisonment were real. And God doesn't rush past any of it. The narrator quietly inserts 'the Lord was with Joseph' in the darkest places — not as a silver lining, but as a structural fact. Providence doesn't mean God prevents pain. It means he is present inside it, working a story you cannot yet read from where you're standing.
days.actionStep: Write a few sentences about a painful chapter of your story. Then write one line underneath it: 'Even here, the Lord was with me.' If you don't believe it yet, write instead: 'I want to believe that. Help me.' Give it to God honestly and leave it there.
days.prayer: God, there have been places in my story where I couldn't feel you. I don't fully understand those chapters yet. But I want to trust that you were there — that you are here — even in the moments that felt most like silence. I'm listening.

days.title: What You Meant for Harm
days.center: Bring to mind someone who has hurt you. You don't have to have resolved anything. Just hold them in mind as you enter this story.
days.watchPrompt: Think back to Joseph's reunion with his brothers at the end of the video. Notice what he says and what he refuses to say. How does the Bible Project connect Joseph's forgiveness to the larger arc of the Genesis promise?
days.reflectionQuestion: Is there someone in your story whose harm you've been carrying — and what would it look like, even one small step, to begin releasing them to God rather than holding them to your own judgment?

scripture.text: Joseph said to his brothers, 'Don't be afraid. Am I in the place of God? You intended harm against me — but God intended it for good, to accomplish what is now happening: the saving of many lives. So don't be afraid. I will provide for you and your children.' And he comforted them, speaking kindly to them.

crossReferences.reason: Jesus makes forgiveness non-optional — the freedom we extend to others is bound to the freedom we receive. Joseph lives this reality before Jesus commands it.
Paul's call to forgive as God has forgiven us is embodied in Joseph — his forgiveness flows from his understanding of what God had done, not from his feelings.
Jesus' prayer of forgiveness from the cross is the fullest expression of what Joseph foreshadowed — evil redeemed through grace rather than returned with retribution.

days.abideInsight: Joseph doesn't pretend the harm wasn't real. He names it directly: 'You intended to harm me.' But he refuses to let human evil define the final meaning of his story. He had found a larger frame — one in which God was the author and redemption was always possible. Forgiveness at this level isn't the same as saying what happened was acceptable. It's choosing to release your hold on another person's debt because you've come to trust that God is the one keeping the books. Joseph's freedom wasn't given to him by his brothers — it was forged in him through years of trusting God in the dark.
days.actionStep: Write a letter you don't have to send — addressed to someone who has caused you real pain. Tell them honestly what they did and how it hurt. Then close it with this: 'I release you to God. I am not your judge.' You don't have to feel it yet. Write it as an act of will, and ask God to make it true in you.
days.prayer: God, I don't always want to forgive. Some of it still hurts. But I don't want to spend my life carrying what you've offered to carry for me. What Joseph chose, I want to choose — not because I'm strong enough, but because you are. Help me release what I've been holding.
